name: The Lantern Cedars of Fukuoji
access: Free, temple grounds open to visitors, but a genuine hillside walk rather than a stroll: the temple sits on Mount Fukuo (495.9m), reached by climbing through the Niomon gate; the cedars stand just past the gate up 53 stone steps, per the temple's own access page.
transport: JR Kabe Line to Kabe Station, then a bus toward Katsuragi (about 10 min) to the Fukuoji-guchi stop, then roughly a 30 minute uphill walk. No public transport reaches the temple itself.
verify_notes: Ensemble entry (one collectible destination, the grove behind the Niomon gate), not a single register row, because no public source distinguishes the individual trees from each other and forcing a register girth onto a named tree would be fabricated precision. History: ja.wikipedia's article on Fukuoji (city-designated natural monument, 市指定天然記念物) cites the Edo-period gazetteer Geihan Tsushi (芸藩通志) recording these cedars; the temple's own site (fukuoji.or.jp/sanpai) states five were planted in 1391 (Meitoku 3) by the Takeda clan during a main-hall reconstruction, under priest Ryokai, and gives height as approximately 37m. Local legend: an epidemic in the district subsided after residents lit lanterns (tomyo) before the trees in prayer, hence Tomyo-sugi, 'Lantern Cedars'; the temple/mountain is also known locally as Aki no Koyasan ('Aki's Mount Koya'). Attrition: one was felled in 1982 for collapse risk (leaving four); the Ministry of Environment's giant-tree register surveyed exactly four specimens here in 2000 (report_id 69359 girth 515cm, 69360 434cm, 69361 395cm, 69362 386cm, all noted 'partial dieback' 一部枯損), consistent with that four-tree state; a further one died and was cut to a 2.2m stump in 2004, per fukuoji.or.jp, leaving three living cedars today, which is what the entry describes. AGE DISCREPANCY, recorded rather than resolved: the ministry register's own survey guessed an age band of only 200-299 years for each of the four 2000-era trees, which conflicts sharply with the documented 1391 planting (roughly 609 years old at the time of that survey). The specific dated planting record from a named Edo-period source is treated here as the stronger evidence and used for age_estimate; the register's shorter band is recorded here rather than silently dropped. Coordinates are the temple grounds from Hiroshima's own tourism site (dive-hiroshima.com), site-level rather than a per-tree survey point; no source gives GPS for the grove itself, hence approximate. Girth 515cm is the largest of the four 2000-survey figures, used as a representative figure for the largest surviving cedar; it should not be read as a specific named tree's exact current girth.

name: The Chichisagari Ginkgo of Nukui Hachiman Shrine
age_estimate: roughly 1,500 years, per its 1979 designation record (not a ring count)

location.address: Nukui Hachiman Shrine, 757 Kawachi-nukui, Asaminami-ku, Hiroshima

access: Free. Shinto shrine grounds, ordinarily open to the public in daylight per the public-religious-ground reading of hard rule 10; no fee, no source records any restriction.
transport: In the Kawachi district of Asaminami-ku, between the Ota and Furukawa rivers; no station within easy walk, nearest access is by car or local bus toward Kawachi from Kobatake or Yokogawa.
verify_notes: Local nickname Chichisagari Icho ('milk-drop ginkgo'), for the large aerial roots hanging from its limbs that resemble breasts, a phenomenon that occurs occasionally on very old ginkgoes. Designated a cultural property in 1979 (Showa 54) per mogurin.or.jp (a Hiroshima cultural-heritage record site); that record states the tree is 'approximately 1,500 years old' but this is the designation's own account rather than a ring count or documented planting, so it is repeated as an estimate with a wide band rather than tightened. GIRTH DISCREPANCY, recorded rather than resolved: mogurin.or.jp gives 5.25m (525cm) and a branch spread of 9.5m E-W / 7m N-S / 6.5m front-back; the Ministry of Environment's giant-tree register (report_id 69345, surveyed 2000) gives 4.18m (418cm) for the same tree. The gap may be different measurement heights or the 21+ years between the two records; both are recorded rather than picking a winner. Height 24m is from mogurin.or.jp only; the register records no height. Coordinates are an OSM place_of_worship node matched to the shrine name (site level, not a tree-level survey point). The district (川内) sits between the Ota and Furukawa rivers and has a documented history of flooding, per the same source, which is context rather than a claim about the tree's own history.
